entries.name: 333 on gold
entries.looks_like: The figures 333, struck alone or in a shaped punch beside other marks.
entries.means: 333 parts of pure gold per 1,000: 8 karat. German law lets jewelry state any fineness in thousandths, which is how 333 is seen.

entries.name: Crown (British gold)
entries.looks_like: A crown in a shaped punch, beside the carat figure (to 1975) or the millesimal number (1975 on).
entries.means: Gold of a British legal standard: with 18 from 1798, with 22 from 1844, on all UK-made gold with 375, 585, 750 or 916 from 1975; optional from 1999. Not used on 9, 12 or 15 carat before 1975.

visual.credit: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; cropped and graded by Heirloom.

entries.name: 18 (British gold, before 1975)
entries.looks_like: The figure 18 in a shaped punch, beside a crown.
entries.means: 18 carat gold (750). The crown and 18 replaced the lion passant on 18 carat gold from 1798; replaced by 750 in 1975.

visual.credit: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; cropped and graded by Heirloom.

entries.name: 22 (British gold, before 1975)
entries.looks_like: The figure 22 in a rectangle with cut corners, struck beside a separate crown.
entries.means: 22 carat gold (916.6). Struck with the crown from 1844; before that 22 carat gold carried the lion passant like sterling.

entries.date_note: Which gold finenesses may appear inside it is not sourced.

entries.looks_like: The imperial crown inside a circle (the sun sign), beside the fineness in thousandths and the firm's name or trademark.
entries.means: German gold of a stated fineness, at least 585, under the 1884 law, from 1 January 1888. Not allowed on jewelry.

entries.name: Soviet star with 583
entries.looks_like: One punch: a Cyrillic assay-office letter, a five-pointed star with hammer and sickle, and the fineness 583.
entries.means: Soviet state assay mark on 583 gold (14 karat at the exact figure). The star type was used from 1958 to 1994.

visual.object: Gold ring, described by its photographer as Soviet
visual.credit: Star61, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; cropped and graded by Heirloom.

entries.single_source: The 1994 end date is from Russia's Federal Assay Chamber only; Postnikova-Loseva (1983) confirms the star mark from 7 May 1958 and 583 as a gold standard.

entries.name: Helvetia head (Swiss gold, 750)
entries.looks_like: A woman's head in profile (Helvetia), with braided hair and a necklace, in a shaped shield; struck with the fineness on watch cases.
entries.means: Swiss official control mark for gold of 750 thousandths (18 karat) on watch cases, a former official hallmark.
entries.date_note: The control lists it among its official hallmarks used since 1880 and since replaced; the end year is not given. Seen on a gold Omega and a gold Rolex case of about 1960 in the Deutsches Uhrenmuseum Furtwangen (47-2966-2, 47-2889-02), beside 18K 0.750.

entries.single_source: Only the Swiss Federal Precious Metals Control's own table of former marks was found; it gives the standard but not the years the mark was used.
